opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a great question, and honestly it's something we thought about a lot before deciding to start the company. I've been working at the intersection of AI and biology for close to a decade now, going back to my time at Facebook AI Research where we worked on protein language models, and then later at Absci. And for most of that time, the honest answer was that these models were really interesting scientifically, but they weren't quite at the point where they could change how drugs actually get discovered.

What shifted, I think, was a few things coming together at once. The first was the AlphaFold moment, which showed that you could take a problem that people had worked on for fifty years, protein structure prediction, and essentially crack it with deep learning. That was a proof point that these methods can learn real physics and real biology from data, not just pattern-match.

But the second thing, and the thing that was really important for us, was the move from predicting single protein structures to modeling interactions: proteins binding to small molecules, to antibodies, to nucleic acids, the whole zoo of molecules that matter for drug discovery. Drugs work by interacting with targets, so if you can model those interactions accurately, you're suddenly much closer to the actual decisions a drug discovery team has to make. The architectures and training recipes had matured to the point where that felt within reach.

And the third piece was just the general progress in AI more broadly: scaling, better generative modeling techniques like diffusion, and the infrastructure to train these systems efficiently. A small, focused team could now build frontier models in this space, which wasn't true even a few years earlier.

So when we looked at all of that, it felt like we were moving from an era where AI could help you understand biology to one where AI could help you engineer it, actually design molecules rather than just analyze them. That's the transition we wanted to build a company around. And we felt strongly that there should be a team that's really obsessed with pushing the frontier of these models and also getting them into the hands of scientists, which is why we released Chai-1 openly early on.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that 2024 was the year where a few threads that had been developing separately for a long time finally came together, and it stopped feeling like a research question and started feeling like an engineering and product question.

If you go back five or six years, protein modeling was really about structure prediction of single chains. AlphaFold 2 was obviously the big moment there, and it was incredible, but a single folded protein by itself doesn't get you a drug. Drugs are about interactions. It's a small molecule sitting in a pocket, an antibody binding an antigen, a protein complexing with another protein. So the question everyone in the field was quietly asking was, can you go from "fold this chain" to "model this whole system of molecules together"?

In parallel, the language model side of things, which is where I spent a lot of my time at Meta on the ESM work, was showing that if you train a big transformer on evolutionary sequence data, it learns a surprising amount about structure and function without ever being told anything explicit about biology. That was a really important signal, because it meant the scaling playbook that worked in NLP had a real analog in biology. More data, more compute, better model, and the improvements were fairly predictable.

And then the third thread was diffusion and generative modeling more broadly. Once you could generate coordinates instead of just classifying or regressing them, you could start thinking about design and not just prediction. So by early 2024 you had multimodal, all-atom models that could reason about proteins, small molecules, nucleic acids, and modifications in one shot, and you had enough evidence that these things scale.

What that meant for us was that the frontier was no longer limited to one or two labs with a unique data asset. It was going to be about building the best team, the best training infrastructure, and getting really tight feedback loops with wet lab experiments. That's a startup-shaped problem. If we'd started two years earlier we'd have been doing research with no clear product, and if we'd waited two more years I think the window would have closed. So 2024 felt like the moment where the science was mature enough to build on, but the field hadn't consolidated yet.

astra-6.text:
I think there were two big shifts. The first was that protein structure prediction showed us that these systems were learnable. You could take something as complicated as a protein sequence and predict its three-dimensional structure with remarkable accuracy. That was a huge proof point for what machine learning could do in biology.

The second shift was moving beyond a single protein in isolation toward modeling how molecules interact. Biology happens through interactions—proteins binding other proteins, small molecules, DNA, RNA. If you want to build useful therapeutics, those are the kinds of systems you need to understand.

By 2024, the progress in biological modeling, combined with advances in generative models and the ability to train at scale, made it feel possible to go after a much broader problem. Could we move from predicting what an existing molecule looks like to designing a molecule that does something we want?

That’s the opportunity behind Chai. Structure prediction is an important foundation, but the goal is to make molecular design more predictable—to connect a desired biological function to a molecule you can actually test in the lab.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there were a few things coming together. The first was that protein structure prediction had shown that you could take a problem in biology that seemed incredibly difficult and make real progress by scaling machine learning. That gave us confidence that these models could learn something fundamental about the physical world.

But predicting the structure of a protein is only part of the picture. Biology happens through interactions—proteins interacting with other proteins, with small molecules, with DNA and RNA. The opportunity was to move toward models that could capture those interactions together, rather than treating each one as a separate problem.

And then the bigger question is: can you go from predicting what an existing molecule does to designing a molecule that does what you want? That’s the connection to drug discovery that’s really exciting. By 2024, the progress in the models, the computational tools, and the ability to test ideas experimentally made it feel like the right moment to build a company around that direction.
